children: Oman and the United Kingdom are exploring closer cooperation in maritime security, logistics and supply-chain resilience, as the two countries seek to strengthen trade and investment ties amid regional uncertainty.

The discussions took place at a high-level economic and commercial roundtable in Westminster during His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik’s state visit to the UK last week. Organised by British Expertise International (BEI) and the Oman British Society (OBS), the meeting brought together Omani officials and British industry specialists to identify opportunities for practical cooperation.
The Omani delegation included representatives from the Financial Services Authority and the Special Economic Zone at Duqm (SEZAD), among others.

The talks focused on maritime risk assessments, insurance frameworks and supply-chain continuity, with participants examining how British expertise could support Oman’s ambitions under Oman Vision 2040 to strengthen its position as a regional hub for trade and investment.

During the state visit, the two countries committed to closer cooperation in security, defence and trade. They are also expected to sign a memorandum of understanding to strengthen maritime cooperation through information-sharing and knowledge exchange with Oman’s Maritime Security Centre.
Dr David Landsman, executive chair of BEI, said British specialists in logistics, maritime security and risk management could help develop industry partnerships with Oman.
“The UK’s wealth of expertise in these fields creates a valuable opportunity to build industry partnerships between the UK and Oman and, ultimately, to strengthen bilateral relations,” he said.
Saleh Zakwani, chair of OBS, said the roundtable reflected the strength of bilateral relations and a shared commitment to resilient trade networks, investment and lasting business partnerships.
Haifa Al Khaifi, secretary general of OBS and a co-moderator of the roundtable, highlighted the significance of Oman’s ports remaining open during a period of regional disruption.

The meeting brought together Omani ports, regulators and industry representatives with British specialists in shipping, insurance, maritime law and risk to identify areas where UK expertise could help strengthen Oman’s role as an Indian Ocean gateway, she said.
Jesal Asher-Rajda, an OBS board member and co-moderator, said the discussions sought to move beyond dialogue towards practical solutions in maritime risk management, insurance and trade resilience.

The roundtable followed talks in May between a senior Omani delegation and UK industry representatives, continuing efforts to identify opportunities for cooperation and investment between the two countries.
